transcript: Welcome to Lesson 3 of Thesis Writing 101. In this video lecture, we dismantle the single most frequent reason proposals get rejected at the Departmental Board of Studies: an ambiguous problem statement.

A research problem is not simply a complaint about society or an expression of personal curiosity. In academic research, a problem exists when there is a documented discrepancy between what current scientific literature predicts and what is actually observed in practice.

To build an airtight problem statement, follow the 3-part framework: First, establish the baseline ideal—what should be happening based on established theory. Second, present the empirical deficit—the documented breakdown, contradiction, or under-researched sector supported by peer-reviewed evidence. Third, define the consequence—what happens if this empirical gap remains unresolved.

When presenting your proposal in Pakistan universities, supervisors often ask: 'Why does this matter in Pakistan specifically?' You must anchor your problem statement with recent, localized contextual data alongside international theoretical foundations.
key: A problem statement is a documented empirical discrepancy, not a personal opinion or broad social complaint.
The 3-part formula: Ideal Baseline (Theory) → Empirical Deficit (Evidence) → Practical Consequence (Urgency).
Always cite peer-reviewed citations within the last 3-5 years to prove your problem is contemporary and unresolved.
Local context must be justified with credible institutional reports (e.g. PBS, SBP, HEC, or industry data).
